The higher-inflation economy must have higher unemployment
Neither can be at its natural rate when inflation is positive
They can be equal despite different inflation rates
question.feedback: A vertical long-run curve permits different inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate once expectations adjust.
question.commonError: Extends the short-run tradeoff to fully expected long-run inflation.

outcomes.label: Analyze expected inflation and supply shocks as Phillips-curve shifters.

question.q: A price-support study predicts more output, then recommends the policy as fair. How should these two claims be evaluated?
options: Test the output prediction separately from the fairness judgment
Ignore the prediction once advice appears
Treat both parts as positive because evidence exists
Treat both parts as normative because policy is involved
question.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
question.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

outcomes.label: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.

question.q: An analyst writes: "A congestion charge will reduce downtown car trips by 10%. That reduction is worth the added financial burden on commuters." How are the two claims classified?
options: First normative; second positive.
Both positive.
First positive; second normative.
Both normative.
question.feedback: The 10% traffic prediction can be tested against evidence, whether or not it proves true. Saying the reduction is worth the burden ranks competing outcomes; that judgment needs a value premise that traffic data alone cannot establish.

outcomes.label: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.

question.q: An economist predicts job losses and recommends against a rule. What additional judgment turns the prediction into policy advice?
options: The existence of a measurable employment effect
The fact that the rule is a government policy
The recommendation adds a value judgment about the predicted cost
The use of an economic forecast.
question.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
question.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

outcomes.label: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.

question.q: A model predicts a tax effect under stated assumptions. Why is it positive?
options: Because the prediction supports the tax
Because the model is written in technical language
Because the prediction must be true if the assumptions are stated.
Evidence could test the conditional prediction
question.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
question.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

outcomes.label: Distinguish testable claims from value judgments.

question.q: A hospital posts the real-time wait at each clinic, and patients shift toward shorter waits. The wait-time information acts like:
options: A price floor.
A guarantee of unlimited capacity.
A nonmonetary signal coordinating demand across locations.
A supply curve shift caused by income.
question.commonError: Failing to recognize nonmoney signals that coordinate scarce capacity.
question.feedback: Information about waiting costs can redirect users much like a price signal.

outcomes.label: Trace price signals through buyer, seller, and resource-allocation decisions

question.q: A bowed-out PPF shows that as more Good X is produced:
options: The opportunity cost of Good X rises
The opportunity cost of Good X falls to zero
The economy escapes scarcity
The PPF becomes a price floor
question.feedback: A bowed-out PPF shows increasing opportunity cost as resources are shifted toward one good.

outcomes.label: Interpret PPF slopes, shapes, and opportunity costs

question.q: Why does opportunity cost usually rise along a bowed-out PPF?
options: Resources are perfectly identical in every use
Resources are not equally well suited to producing both goods
Scarcity disappears at high output levels
Prices are fixed by government
question.feedback: Opportunity cost rises because resources are specialized and become less well suited as they are shifted into the other good.

outcomes.label: Interpret PPF slopes, shapes, and opportunity costs

question.q: An economy is producing inside its PPF. What is the best interpretation?
options: The point is unattainable
The point is efficient
The point is attainable but inefficient
The point eliminates scarcity
question.feedback: A point inside the PPF can be produced, but resources are not being used efficiently.

outcomes.label: Analyze feasible production, efficiency, and changes in capacity

question.q: A workshop makes chairs and desks. Better scheduling lets previously idle machines produce more of both until no further increase in either is possible without reducing the other. Labor, machines and technology are unchanged. How does this appear on its PPF?
options: An outward shift of the frontier.
A move from one frontier point to another.
A move beyond the unchanged frontier.
A move from inside to the unchanged frontier.
question.feedback: Idle machines initially put production inside the PPF. Using existing capacity fully moves production to the frontier. The unchanged resources and technology mean capacity has not expanded, so the frontier does not shift.

outcomes.label: Analyze feasible production, efficiency, and changes in capacity

question.q: An economy gains more capital and better technology. What happens to its PPF?
options: It shifts outward
It shifts inward
It becomes a demand curve
It creates a binding price floor
question.feedback: More resources or better technology increase productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

outcomes.label: Analyze feasible production, efficiency, and changes in capacity

question.q: A natural disaster destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the PPF?
options: It shifts outward
It shifts inward
The economy moves to a different point on the same PPF.
Opportunity cost disappears
question.feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

outcomes.label: Analyze feasible production, efficiency, and changes in capacity

question.q: Moving along a PPF gives up 18 units of Good Y to gain 6 units of Good X. What is the opportunity cost per unit of Good X?
options: 6 units of Good Y
18 units of Good Y
3 units of Good Y
108 units of Good Y
question.feedback: Opportunity cost per Good X is what is given up divided by what is gained: 18 / 6 = 3.

outcomes.label: Interpret PPF slopes, shapes, and opportunity costs

question.q: A PPF move gains 5 units of Good X but gives up 20 units of Good Y. What is the opportunity cost per additional Good X?
options: 5 units of Good Y
20 units of Good Y
0.25 units of Good Y
4 units of Good Y
question.feedback: The economy gives up 20 units of Good Y to gain 5 units of Good X, so 20 / 5 = 4.

outcomes.label: Interpret PPF slopes, shapes, and opportunity costs

question.commonError: Multiplies output by productivity instead of dividing.
question.q: A team must produce 2,400 units. Productivity improves from 8 to 10 units per hour. How many labor hours are now needed?
options: 192 hours
240 hours
300 hours
24,000 hours
question.feedback: Required hours=output/productivity=2400/10=240, down from 300.

outcomes.label: Calculate output per worker and interpret productivity changes.

question.q: Money grows 6 percent, velocity is stable, and output grows 2 percent. Approximate inflation is:
options: 4 percent
6 percent
8 percent
2 percent
question.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth minus output growth: 6 - 2 = 4 percent.

outcomes.label: Connect money growth, output growth, velocity, and inflation

question.q: If M = 200, V = 5, and Y = 500, then P equals:
question.feedback: MV = PY, so 200 x 5 = P x 500, which gives P = 2.

outcomes.label: Apply the quantity equation and interpret money-market adjustment

question.q: The price level rises from 2 to 5. Using value of money=1/P, how many units of the reference basket can $10 buy afterward?
options: 2 units
5 units
20 units
50 units
question.feedback: At P=5 each dollar buys 1/5 basket unit; 10/5=2 units.
question.commonError: Multiplies cash by the price level to measure purchasing power.

outcomes.label: Apply the quantity equation and interpret money-market adjustment

question.commonError: Uses the value-of-money fraction directly as the basket price.
question.q: Money’s value falls from 1/2 to 1/4 basket unit per dollar. What happens to the dollars needed to buy one unchanged basket?
options: They rise from $0.50 to $0.75
They stay $2 because the basket is unchanged
They rise from $2 to $4
They fall from $4 to $2
question.feedback: The basket price is the reciprocal of money’s value: 2 then 4.

outcomes.label: Apply the quantity equation and interpret money-market adjustment

question.commonError: Ignores a stated change in velocity.
question.q: Use the quantity-theory growth approximation. Money grows 12% and output 4%. If velocity now falls 2% rather than staying stable, what inflation rate is predicted?
question.feedback: Inflation≈gM+gV−gY=12−2−4=6%. The velocity decline lowers spending growth.

outcomes.label: Connect money growth, output growth, velocity, and inflation

items.topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power

question.q: A real appreciation makes domestic goods relatively more expensive. How does this connect to net exports?
options: Exports tend to rise because domestic goods cost more
Imports tend to fall because foreign goods become relatively cheaper
Exports tend to fall and imports tend to rise, reducing NX
Exports and imports both rise by equal amounts
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Exports tend to rise because domestic goods cost more” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
question.feedback: A higher real exchange rate shifts spending toward foreign goods, lowering exports minus imports.

outcomes.label: Calculate real exchange rates and evaluate purchasing-power parity as a long-run benchmark.

question.commonError: Multiplies nominal GDP by the price index instead of deflating.
question.q: Nominal GDP is $180 and the GDP deflator is 120 (base 100). What real GDP value makes the output comparison use base-year prices?
question.feedback: Real GDP=nominal GDP/(deflator/100)=180/1.2=150.

outcomes.label: Distinguish nominal and real GDP and calculate the GDP deflator.

question.commonError: Uses the current price instead of the base-year price to value current output.
question.q: An economy produces only one good. In the base year its price is $5 and quantity is 100. In the next year price is $6 and quantity is 110. What is next-year real GDP measured at base-year prices?
question.feedback: Real GDP uses current quantity at the base-year price: 110×$5=$550. Using $6 gives nominal GDP $660; holding quantity at 100 would miss the real production increase.

outcomes.label: Distinguish nominal and real GDP and calculate the GDP deflator.

question.commonError: Uses expected inflation for a realized real return.
question.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan fixes nominal interest at 9%. Expected inflation was 5%, but actual inflation is 7%. What realized real rate replaces the expected 4%?
question.feedback: Realized real interest≈9−7=2%; actual, rather than expected, inflation determines realized purchasing power.

outcomes.label: Calculate and interpret real and nominal interest rates.

question.q: A disinflation’s annual output losses are 1% and 3% of one year’s output. Inflation falls 2 percentage points. What is the sacrifice ratio?
question.feedback: Add losses 1+3=4 and divide by the 2-point inflation reduction: 4/2=2.
question.commonError: Averages annual losses instead of summing cumulative output loss.

outcomes.label: Calculate and interpret output losses associated with disinflation.

question.q: Expected inflation falls faster after a credible announcement. How can that connect to the sacrifice ratio?
options: A lower final inflation rate automatically raises the ratio even with unchanged loss
Credibility changes the denominator from inflation reduction to unemployment
The ratio must become zero in every credible disinflation plan
A smaller cumulative output loss can lower the measured ratio
question.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.
question.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.

outcomes.label: Calculate and interpret output losses associated with disinflation.

question.q: Two plans each reduce inflation 4 percentage points. Plan A has sacrifice ratio 2; Plan B has ratio 1.5. Which has the lower estimated cumulative output loss?
options: Both: 4% because the inflation targets match
B: 1.5% versus A: 2% regardless of the size of disinflation
B: 6% versus A: 8% of annual output
A: 2% versus B: 2.67% of annual output
question.feedback: Loss=ratio×inflation reduction. A: 2×4=8;B: 1.5×4=6.
question.commonError: Compares ratio levels without scaling by the inflation reduction.

outcomes.label: Calculate and interpret output losses associated with disinflation.

question.q: How does household saving connect to later capital formation?
options: Saving is itself always a newly produced capital good
Saved funds must remain idle outside all markets
Financial channels can direct saved funds to investment projects
Capital formation occurs only through household consumption
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Saving is itself always a newly produced capital good” in this saving and investment identities task.
question.feedback: The financial system connects the repaired saving idea to firms and households that borrow for new capital investment.

outcomes.label: Apply private, public, and national saving identities and the saving-investment relationship.

question.q: How does positive public saving connect the accounting identities to the loanable-funds market?
options: It shifts investment demand by definition
It adds to national saving, the supply of loanable funds
It makes private saving equal zero
It converts government purchases into consumption
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It shifts investment demand by definition” in this saving and investment identities task.
question.feedback: Public saving joins private saving to form national saving, which supplies funds in the closed-economy loanable-funds model.

outcomes.label: Apply private, public, and national saving identities and the saving-investment relationship.

question.q: How does the accounting identity connect to the loanable-funds model?
options: Consumption becomes the demand for loanable funds
Government purchases become the real interest rate
Every saver chooses the same investment project
National saving supplies funds that finance aggregate investment
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Consumption becomes the demand for loanable funds” in this saving and investment identities task.
question.feedback: The closed-economy identity provides the aggregate connection; the loanable-funds market explains coordination through the real interest rate.

outcomes.label: Apply private, public, and national saving identities and the saving-investment relationship.

question.q: A library extends weekend hours but must reduce weekday staffing. What does this demonstrate?
options: A market surplus
The end of scarcity
A tradeoff in the use of limited staff time.
A guarantee that everyone benefits equally.
question.commonError: Failing to transfer the tradeoff idea to a service setting.
question.feedback: More staffing in one period leaves less staffing available in another.

outcomes.label: Identify scarcity, tradeoffs, and opportunity cost

question.q: A food bank receives more donations but still cannot meet every request. Which conclusion is best?
options: The food bank now faces only a temporary shortage
The additional resources reduce the constraint but do not eliminate scarcity.
No allocation rule is needed once donations increase
Scarcity disappears whenever supply increases.
question.commonError: Assuming more resources remove all unmet wants.
question.feedback: More resources can ease scarcity while competing needs remain.

outcomes.label: Identify scarcity, tradeoffs, and opportunity cost

question.q: A campus uses its only open parcel for a laboratory instead of student housing. Scarcity creates a tradeoff; which concept names the next-best alternative forgone?
options: Opportunity cost
Market equilibrium
Price elasticity
Monetary neutrality
question.commonError: Recognizing a tradeoff without connecting it to the next-best forgone alternative.
question.feedback: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up when scarcity forces a choice.

outcomes.label: Identify scarcity, tradeoffs, and opportunity cost

question.q: A factory divides fixed labor and machine time between medical devices and water filters. Which model displays the feasible production combinations created by this scarcity?
options: A production possibilities frontier
A consumer price index
A money-demand curve
A Phillips curve
question.commonError: Recognizing limited resources without connecting them to feasible production combinations.
question.feedback: A PPF represents the combinations possible when scarce productive resources have competing uses.

outcomes.label: Identify scarcity, tradeoffs, and opportunity cost

question.q: Expected prices rise and new wage contracts raise nominal costs. With aggregate demand fixed, apply the SRAS shift to output and the price level.
options: Output rises and the price level falls
Output and the price level both fall
Output falls and the price level rises
Output and the price level both rise
question.feedback: Higher expected wages/costs shift SRAS left. The intersection with unchanged AD has lower output and higher prices.
question.commonError: Treats higher expected costs as an increase in short-run supply.

outcomes.label: Analyze the SRAS slope, expected prices, input costs, productivity, and short-run aggregate-supply shifts.

question.q: If nominal wages are sticky and the price level rises unexpectedly, firms' real labor costs:
options: Fall, so output rises
Rise, so output falls
Stay fixed forever
Become money demand
question.feedback: Sticky nominal wages mean a higher price level lowers real labor costs and can raise output.

outcomes.label: Analyze the SRAS slope, expected prices, input costs, productivity, and short-run aggregate-supply shifts.

question.q: Oil costs fall while aggregate demand is unchanged. What output/price combination follows from the resulting SRAS shift?
options: Both output and the price level rise
Output falls and the price level rises
Both output and the price level fall
Output rises and the price level falls
question.feedback: Lower input costs shift SRAS right, increasing output and reducing the price level at the new demand intersection.
question.commonError: Uses demand-shift price/output signs for a supply improvement.

outcomes.label: Analyze the SRAS slope, expected prices, input costs, productivity, and short-run aggregate-supply shifts.

question.q: Aggregate demand expands unexpectedly, raising output and the price level. What short-run change in unemployment and inflation does the Phillips-curve model predict?
options: Lower unemployment and higher inflation along the current SRPC
Higher unemployment and higher inflation from an SRPC shift
Lower unemployment and lower inflation from an LRPC shift
Unchanged unemployment with a downward SRPC shift
question.feedback: With expected inflation initially fixed, a demand change moves the economy along the current SRPC.
question.commonError: Shifts the entire SRPC when aggregate demand changes unexpectedly.

outcomes.label: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation–unemployment tradeoff.

question.q: An SRPC predicts 4% inflation at 5% unemployment. Expected inflation then rises 2 percentage points; in this model it shifts the SRPC up one-for-one, with other supply conditions unchanged. At 5% unemployment, what inflation and curve change follow?
options: 6% inflation; an upward shift of the SRPC
6% inflation; movement along the original SRPC
2% inflation; a downward shift of the SRPC
4% inflation; no shift because unemployment is unchanged
question.feedback: At the same unemployment rate, the two-point expectations increase adds two points to predicted inflation: 4+2=6%. Changing inflation at fixed unemployment locates a shifted curve, not movement along the old curve.
question.commonError: Calls a change in inflation at fixed unemployment a movement along an unchanged SRPC.

outcomes.label: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation–unemployment tradeoff.

question.q: A demand surprise briefly reduces unemployment from 5% to 4%. Natural unemployment is unchanged. Once expectations fully adjust, what rate is the long-run benchmark?
question.feedback: With no change in natural unemployment, the surprise cannot permanently sustain 4%; the long-run benchmark remains 5%.
question.commonError: Treats a temporary demand-driven unemployment gain as a lower natural rate.

outcomes.label: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation–unemployment tradeoff.

question.q: A contraction lowers inflation from 6% to 4% along a fixed SRPC. In the short run, what unemployment change should accompany that disinflation?
options: Natural unemployment automatically falls 2 points
Unemployment rises
Unemployment falls
Unemployment must stay fixed
question.feedback: A movement down a fixed downward-sloping SRPC entails higher unemployment as inflation falls. It does not itself change the natural rate.
question.commonError: Claims disinflation along a fixed SRPC has no unemployment cost.

outcomes.label: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation–unemployment tradeoff.

question.commonError: Confuses a higher starting level with a higher marginal return.
question.q: Two countries share technology and worker skills, but A has much less capital per worker. Both add the same small amount of capital per worker. With diminishing marginal returns, which comparison follows?
options: B gains more because its starting output is higher
Both gain the same because additions are equal
A loses output because it began with less capital
A gains more output per worker from that addition
question.feedback: Under comparable other conditions, capital is more productive at the margin where it is scarcer. This is conditional catch-up potential.

outcomes.label: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

question.commonError: Confuses identical physical inputs with equal marginal products.
question.q: With labor and technology fixed, successive identical machines raise output by 12, 9 and 6 units. A plan assumes a fourth adds 12. Which revision fits diminishing marginal returns?
options: Expect a gain smaller than 6 if the pattern continues
Expect a gain of 12 because the machines are identical
Expect total output to fall by 6
Expect every previous machine’s output to disappear
question.feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concern successively smaller additions to output, not a fall in total output or identical gains from identical inputs.

outcomes.label: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

question.commonError: Treats physical capital as productive without complementary worker skills.
question.q: A factory buys machines but cannot operate them because workers lack the necessary training. Which complementary change would make the physical-capital investment usable?
options: Count the machines as natural resources
Raise product prices without changing production
Train workers to operate the new machines
Replace worker training with more idle machines
question.feedback: Training supplies complementary human capital, allowing the new physical capital to contribute to output.

outcomes.label: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

question.commonError: Equates resource discovery with immediate usable output.
question.q: A mineral deposit is discovered, but output cannot rise until transport links reach it. Which conclusion applies the natural-resource distinction?
options: Only human capital changed because discovery involves knowledge
The deposit is produced capital because it has economic value
Resource availability improved, but complementary infrastructure is needed to use it
Current productivity must already have risen by the full value of the deposit
question.feedback: The natural resource exists, but access requires produced infrastructure. A resource discovery is not itself measured production or guaranteed immediate productivity.

outcomes.label: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

question.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
question.q: Workers receive better machines but no extra labor is added. What should happen to productivity, other things equal?
options: It should rise
It must fall
It becomes CPI
It becomes unemployment
question.feedback: More or better capital helps workers produce more.

outcomes.label: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

question.commonError: Attributes every productivity gain to more physical capital.
question.q: A new production method raises output with the same workforce and machines. If the method is shared with a comparable second plant, what change could occur without more physical capital?
options: Only its number of machines could rise
Its output per worker must fall
Only its nominal selling price could change
Its output per worker could rise
question.feedback: Using a better method can raise productivity at unchanged inputs; technology is distinct from adding machines.

outcomes.label: Analyze physical capital, human capital, natural resources, and technology.

question.q: After a demand recession, falling wages are already shifting SRAS right toward recovery. A stimulus takes a year to arrive. What fact is most relevant to whether it will stabilize output at arrival?
options: Only the size of the gap when the recession began
Whether the original shock was measured in dollars
Whether the economy has ever used fiscal policy before
The expected remaining gap when the stimulus arrives
question.feedback: Compare the intervention with conditions at implementation. Existing self-correction can reduce or eliminate the gap before delayed stimulus arrives.
question.commonError: Targets a historical gap without allowing for recovery during the policy lag.

outcomes.label: Choose and evaluate policy responses to output gaps

question.q: Rates are near zero and additional money barely changes investment. Officials propose another identical monetary expansion solely to stimulate investment. Which forecast follows from the stated constraint?
options: A guaranteed rise in interest and fall in money supply
A direct improvement in technology independent of spending
A limited additional investment response
A guaranteed large response because every reserve dollar becomes investment
question.feedback: The weak rate/spending channel limits the same instrument’s extra demand effect in the stated near-zero-rate setting.
question.commonError: Treats monetary expansion as a guaranteed large investment stimulus despite a binding transmission limit.

outcomes.label: Evaluate policy lags, automatic stabilizers, and supply-shock tradeoffs

question.q: A stimulus approved during recession arrives after output has returned to potential. With no new negative shock, which risk follows from the implementation lag?
options: It lowers potential output by changing the approval date
It can push demand above capacity
It automatically reverses direction and contracts demand
It is costless because the initial recession justified it
question.feedback: The demand addition arrives after its original gap has closed and can create excess demand.
question.commonError: Assesses policy only at approval rather than implementation.

outcomes.label: Evaluate policy lags, automatic stabilizers, and supply-shock tradeoffs

question.commonError: Not comparing stimulus size to the recessionary gap.
question.q: A recessionary AD gap is $300 billion. Policy raises spending by $75 billion and the multiplier is 4. What happens?
options: The gap closes exactly
A $75 billion gap remains
AD overshoots by $75 billion
The gap is unchanged
question.feedback: $75 billion x 4 = $300 billion, so the gap closes exactly.

outcomes.label: Choose and evaluate policy responses to output gaps

question.commonError: Stops with an AD shift and does not connect the short-run output response to unemployment and inflation pressure.
question.q: Contractionary stabilization policy shifts AD left to cool an overheating economy. Which short-run labor-market effect connects this policy choice to Phillips-curve analysis?
options: Unemployment tends to rise as output weakens while inflation pressure falls.
Unemployment must fall because lower AD always increases hiring.
Unemployment is unchanged because only the price level responds to AD.
The natural rate permanently falls by the size of the AD shift.
question.feedback: A contractionary stabilization policy that lowers AD can reduce inflation pressure while raising unemployment in the short run, creating the bridge to Phillips-curve analysis.

outcomes.label: Choose and evaluate policy responses to output gaps

question.q: A $4 tax on buyers and a $4 tax on sellers create the same wedge in the same market. What should happen to the market outcome?
options: The outcome should be equivalent
The buyer tax must hurt only buyers
The seller tax must hurt only sellers
Only the seller tax reduces quantity
question.feedback: Equivalent taxes on buyers or sellers create the same wedge and market outcome.

outcomes.label: Distinguish legal tax assignment from economic burden.

question.q: A student says, 'If sellers legally pay the tax, buyers avoid the burden.' What is wrong?
options: Elasticities, not legal labels, determine burden
The statement is always correct
Sellers cannot change prices
Taxes do not affect buyers
question.feedback: Legal assignment does not determine who bears the economic burden.

outcomes.label: Distinguish legal tax assignment from economic burden.

question.q: Bread's selling price rises, while flour becomes cheaper. Considering each change separately, how does it affect the supply of bread?
options: Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply right.
Higher bread price shifts supply right; cheaper flour moves sellers along supply.
Higher bread price moves sellers along supply; cheaper flour shifts supply left.
Both changes move sellers along the same supply curve.
question.feedback: Bread's own price changes quantity supplied along a supply curve. Flour is a production input: a lower flour price reduces cost at each output level, shifting bread supply right. These are separate mechanisms.

outcomes.label: Apply the law of supply and distinguish movements from shifts

question.q: The price of concert tickets falls, and venues offer fewer tickets for resale. Which statement is most precise?
options: Quantity supplied decreased, but supply did not necessarily shift
Supply decreased because price changed
Demand increased because price fell
Supply shifted right because sellers offered fewer tickets
question.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

outcomes.label: Apply the law of supply and distinguish movements from shifts

question.q: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens in the shoe market?
options: Supply increases
Supply decreases
Demand increases
Quantity demanded decreases
question.feedback: Better technology lowers production costs, shifting supply right.

outcomes.label: Analyze supply shifters, aggregation, and combined market effects

question.q: Delivery firms face higher diesel prices and also receive higher prices for each delivery. Consider each change separately. Which change reduces delivery supply at every delivery price?
options: Higher delivery prices; they shift delivery supply left.
Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply right.
Higher diesel prices; they shift delivery supply left.
Higher delivery prices; they move firms down the supply curve.
question.feedback: Diesel is an input. Its higher price raises the cost of making deliveries, so firms offer fewer at each delivery price: supply shifts left. A higher price received per delivery instead increases quantity supplied along a curve.

outcomes.label: Analyze supply shifters, aggregation, and combined market effects

question.q: A tax causes buyers to pay $5 more and sellers to receive $2 less. Which side likely has less elastic behavior?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Neither side
The government
question.feedback: The side bearing more of the tax is usually less elastic. Buyers bear $5, so demand is likely less elastic.

outcomes.label: Use relative elasticity to determine who bears a tax

question.q: Supply is less elastic than demand. Who is expected to bear more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Both sides bear zero
Only the legal taxpayer
question.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic, sellers bear more.

outcomes.label: Use relative elasticity to determine who bears a tax

question.q: Before a tax, buyers pay $20 and sellers receive $20. After the tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. What is the tax per unit?
question.feedback: The tax wedge is buyer price minus seller price: $24 - $18 = $6.

outcomes.label: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.

question.q: A tax raises the price buyers pay and lowers the price sellers receive. What else usually happens?
options: Quantity traded falls
Quantity traded rises
Scarcity disappears
The PPF shifts outward
question.feedback: A tax creates a wedge and reduces the quantity traded.

outcomes.label: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.

question.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
question.q: A discouraged worker starts applying for jobs again but does not find one. What happens?
options: They become unemployed
They become employed
They leave the labor force
They are counted as retired
question.feedback: Active job search moves the worker into the labor force as unemployed.

outcomes.label: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.

question.commonError: Incorrect inference: Employment: falls 1; unemployment: rises 1.
question.q: A survey has 90 employed and 10 unemployed. One employed person cuts paid work to one hour while seeking full-time work. How do measured employment and unemployment change?
options: Employment: falls 1; unemployment: rises 1.
Employment: rises 1; unemployment: falls 1.
Employment: unchanged; unemployment: unchanged.
Employment: falls 1; unemployment: unchanged.
question.feedback: One paid hour still counts as employed under the stated status rule. Underemployment changes without changing these measured counts.

outcomes.label: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.

question.commonError: Keeps discouraged nonsearchers in the labor force.
question.q: There are 90 employed and 10 unemployed. Four unemployed people stop searching; nobody else changes status. What is the new labor force?
question.feedback: The four move from unemployed to outside the labor force.90+6=96; employment stays 90.

outcomes.label: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.

question.commonError: Excludes active unemployed job seekers from participation.
question.q: Adult population is 250 and the labor force 150. Ten previously nonparticipating adults start active job search without finding jobs. What is the new LFPR?
question.feedback: Job seekers join the labor force: 160/250=64%. They need not already be employed to participate.

outcomes.label: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.

question.commonError: Reduces the labor-force denominator when an unemployed worker becomes employed.
question.q: There are 152 employed and 8 unemployed. Two unemployed workers find jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
question.feedback: The labor force stays 160 while unemployment becomes 6: 6/160=3.75%.

outcomes.label: Classify labor-force status and calculate unemployment and participation rates.

question.commonError: Attributes recession layoffs to a permanent skill mismatch.
question.q: Sales fall economy-wide during recession and trained workers are laid off. If demand returns with skills still suitable, which unemployment component should most directly shrink?
options: Cyclical unemployment
Structural unemployment from obsolete skills
Frictional unemployment from voluntary job changes
Natural unemployment caused by permanent skill mismatch
question.feedback: The unemployment arose from weak aggregate demand rather than an enduring mismatch; recovery can reduce its cyclical component.

outcomes.label: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.

question.commonError: Confuses job matching with structural skill mismatch.
question.q: Two workers are unemployed: A is briefly between suitable jobs; B’s old occupation has disappeared and employers require skills B lacks. Which worker is more directly helped by retraining?
options: A, because all job search is structural mismatch
Both equally, because duration alone defines unemployment type
Neither, because training can affect only cyclical unemployment
B, because the problem is structural mismatch
question.feedback: B lacks the skills demanded in available jobs. A’s short search between suitable jobs is frictional; faster matching may help without retraining.

outcomes.label: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.

question.commonError: Assumes demand expansion directly removes a skill mismatch.
question.q: Automation removes jobs whose workers lack skills for new vacancies. A policy only boosts demand for output without changing skills. Which limit follows?
options: The skill mismatch may persist despite stronger demand
All mismatch disappears as soon as spending increases
Unemployment becomes frictional solely because demand rises
The workers leave the labor force automatically
question.feedback: More demand need not give displaced workers the skills needed for existing vacancies. A structural problem can require retraining or mobility.

outcomes.label: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.

question.q: A jobless worker has actively applied for jobs this week after voluntarily leaving a suitable job. Is this worker officially counted as unemployed, and which type of unemployment best describes the situation?
options: Counted as unemployed, with frictional unemployment as the likely type
Not in the labor force, with structural unemployment as the likely type
Counted as employed, with cyclical unemployment as the likely type
Not counted in labor statistics because leaving a job voluntarily prevents unemployment status
question.commonError: Using the cause of unemployment to decide official employment status, or using official status without identifying the unemployment type.
question.feedback: Active job search makes the worker officially unemployed; normal search after leaving a suitable job is frictional unemployment.

outcomes.label: Distinguish frictional, structural, and cyclical unemployment.
